comment.value:
The paper introduces NORMWEAR, a multimodal foundation model for wearable sensor data designed to handle heterogeneous sensor configurations and generalize across diverse health tasks. It employs CWT-based tokenization for modality-agnostic preprocessing, shared-weight intra-channel encoders with a channel-aware [CLS] token for inter-sensor fusion, and a memory stream temporal fusion module aligned with textual descriptions to enable zero-shot inference. Pretrained on 2.5 million sensor segments from multiple modalities (e.g., PPG, ECG, EEG, GSR, IMU), NORMWEAR is evaluated on 18 tasks across 11 public datasets and achieves state-of-the-art results in zero-, partial-, and full-shot settings, outperforming handcrafted baselines, deep time-series models, and modality-specific foundation models.

Strengths:
1. The work is first of its kind to introduce a foundation model across heterogeneous wearable physiological modalities

2. Extensive evaluation and strong empirical results.

Weakness:

1. Added complexity without clear gain Combining first- and second-order derivatives with CWT increases computational complexity, yet the authors provide no strong theoretical or broad empirical justification beyond application-specific references. Authors claim that this makes the spectrum “more sensitive to rapid signal changes” is unconvincing, as CWT inherently captures high-frequency components by design.

2. Risk of information loss Resampling all signals to 65 Hz seems arbitrary, especially for ECG and EEG where higher frequency content is important. The rebuttal relies on weak references, and in my experience, many ECG datasets capture up to ~50 Hz or more, making the resampling choice questionable.

3. Limited novelty The “channel-adaptive” property applies a shared backbone to each channel. This is straightforward and not a significant architectural advance.


During the rebuttal, the authors: 

(1) added mathematical formulations to clarify the engineering details of the channel-aware and memory stream–inspired fusion mechanisms; 

(2) provided a deeper discussion of the trade-offs between modality-specific and generic modeling approaches; 

(3) included additional ablations evaluating STFT and CWT (without derivatives) as alternative initial embeddings; 

(4) carefully proofread the manuscript to correct typos and improve overall clarity.

Some reviewer still has major concerns that were not adequately addressed, while others remain neutral toward the paper. Therefore, I recommend rejection.

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful engagement and recognition of the significance of the challenges addressed in this work. We are encouraged that three of the four reviewers rated this work positively, acknowledging our success in tackling key challenges in the field, mainly NormWear’s ability to process heterogeneous wearable sensor signals invariants to their modality, channel count, and order. As the reviewers agree, our extensive experiments have shown that Normwear has excelled in a wide range of health-related tasks, highlighting its generalizability and practical impact. We are pleased that, during the rebuttal and discussion, we were able to address all the questions and concerns from reviewers lush, CapQ, and qdb8.

While we respect all perspectives, we hope our additions, which directly address qamC's stated reservations, can help resolve the remaining concerns.

In closing, we believe that the reviewers and our team share a common vision for the future of this field. We are deeply grateful for the reviewers’ guidance, which has been invaluable to us. Through this process, we have envisioned the potential of a unified model for physiological sensors and hope that our efforts will ultimately contribute to the growth and advancement of this promising direction.

Best,
Authors

## 1) Response to the question on the shape of the output from our first attention

We apologize for the confusion, our original phrasing **``$z_i \in \mathbb{R}^E$ as the deep-copied version…”** may have implied that $z_i$ referred to the input token rather than the output after intra-channel attention. We have revised this to: **“$z = [CLS] \in \mathbb{R}^E$, which is deep-copied and prepended at each input channel,”** to better reflect the intended meaning. Specifically, we described earlier that $z = [CLS] \in \mathbb{R}^E$, which is the special token prepended to each input channel. Here, $Q(z) \in \mathbb{R}^E$ is a vector, as we only intended to show the operation applied to a single [CLS] token. In contrast, the standard multi-token attention operation uses $Q(z_{all}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times E}$. We hope this revision and clarification help improve clarity.

We have updated all equations by replacing `softmax` with `\text{softmax}`, and we now use `\left` and `\right` to properly scale parentheses around the fraction.

We thank the reviewer for their follow-up. We are encouraged that our earlier response resolved several concerns, including (i) the advantage of CWT over STFT, (ii) the design rationale and efficiency of our channel-aware attention, and (iii) the structure and complexity of our zero-shot evaluation pipeline. Below we respond to the remaining points.
# 1) Motivation of the derivative accompanied with CWT
Mathematically, if a signal $x(t)$ represents the raw physiological signal, its first derivative $\frac{dx(t)}{dt}$ captures the rate of change, while the second derivative $\frac{d^2x(t)}{dt^2}$ captures the acceleration of changes. 
The Fourier Transform of the $n$th derivative of a signal is given by: 
$$\hat{f^n}(\xi) = F(\frac{d^n x(t)}{dt^n}) = (i 2 \pi \xi)^n \hat{f}(\xi)$$

where $\hat{f^n}(\xi)$ is the Fourier transform of $x(t)$. This shows that differentiation amplifies higher frequencies, making the spectrum more sensitive to rapid signal changes. Similarly, for continuous wavelet transformation on the first and second order derivative of $x(t)$ [4], we can emphasize the sudden high frequency physiological events, such as QRS complexes in ECG, dicrotic notches in PPG, and epileptic spikes in EEG, by capturing localized temporal dynamics. This derivative-based preprocessing strategy is well-established in both physiological and audio signal analysis [5–6], offering strong performance at minimal computational cost. To clarify the model complexity, we include below a GFLOPs comparison, a standard metric in ML, to highlight the negligible computational overhead with a moderate performance benefit. We hope these theoretical insights, along with supporting empirical evidence below, adequately address the reviewer’s concern.
|Method|Activity Recognition|EEG Tasks|Risk Evaluation|Vital Signs|Micro Avg.|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|
| NormWear - CWT w/ derivatives (51.50 GFLOPs/sample)|**83.102**|**85.883**|**73.165**|**95.375**|**82.762**|
| NormWear - CWT w/o derivatives (51.34 GFLOPs/sample)|82.093|81.522|70.922|95.064|80.341|
# 2) Concern on the sampling rate
We sample all modalities to 65 Hz to enable unified tokenization while preserving essential frequency components across modalities, all of which lie well below the Nyquist frequency (i.e., 32.5 Hz). For example, human movement patterns typically lie below 30 Hz [1], heart rate variability (HRV) features appear under 5 Hz, and ECG signals mainly concentrate in the 0.5–30 Hz range [2]; EEG rhythms, including delta (0.1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (14–30 Hz), and lower gamma, are similarly retained [3].

While some very specific use cases may benefit from higher sampling rates, our study shows that 65 Hz is sufficient to support diverse health and behavior modeling tasks across modalities for a general purpose foundation model. Future work may explore whether the finer-grained dynamics captured by higher sampling rates offer advantages despite increased computational cost.
# 3) The contribution on the channel-aware mechanism
We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s suggestion that simplicity of implementation diminishes the significance of a contribution. Many foundational techniques in machine learning, such as residual connection or contrastive loss, are straightforward to implement but are valued for their strong motivation, conceptual novelty, and real-world impact. We thank the reviewer for the insightful and constructive comments. We have proofread the manuscript and corrected the typo issues. We provide the detailed point-to-point response to the questions and weakness below:

# Response to Questions
## 1) Hours of PPG-DaLiA
Thank you for raising this point. While the original PPG-DaLiA dataset contains about 36 hours of data, the 71 hours in Table 5 reflect the total duration after preprocessing with 6-second windows and 50% overlap, which doubles the data. This is a common practice in IMU preprocessing [1], and we will clarify this in the appendix. This is the only pretrained dataset that leverage the overlap setting, and we will correct the length to 36 hours. 

## 2) Question on EEG channel of a downstreaming task
Thank you for the question. Fig. 15 uses a leading-channel EEG sample from the Epileptic Seizure Recognition dataset used by TF-C [2], detailed in Appendix A. Our model does not rely on any single patch for tumor-related features; instead, predictions aggregate information across all patches. As shown in Fig. 15, while all patches contribute, those with peaks or distinct variations tend to receive higher weights.

## 3) Mismatch of sampling rate
We thank the reviewer for the question. Although the CWT transformation does not inherently standardize sampling rates across modalities, we explicitly resampled all signals to 65 Hz prior to applying CWT and tokenization. We selected 65 Hz because it captures the relevant frequency ranges across all modalities considered. This includes physiological signals such as cardiac activity, human motion, and neural activity up to the lower gamma band (above 30 Hz), as described in Appendix B.1.

# Response to Weakness
## 1) Why use differentiation with CWT?
We thank the reviewer for raising this practical point. Including first- and second-order derivatives is motivated by both empirical findings and the properties of physiological signals. Prior work shows that derivatives help transformers capture transient or subtle dynamics, especially in noisy or complex settings [3–4]. In our case, derivatives are appended as additional feature channels to each signal segment and processed jointly with the raw input. This increases dimensionality per spatial-temporal location but preserves the input’s temporal structure. Since the convolutional tokenizer patchifies only across temporal and spectral dimensions, the number of resulting tokens remains unaffected by the added channels. As a result, the model’s overall computational complexity, in Big-O terms, remains unchanged.

## 2) CWT introduces hyperparameters why not STFT?
We thank the reviewer for raising this valuable point regarding STFT-based tokenization. As discussed in Section 3.2, our core motivation for using Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) over Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) is that STFT imposes a fixed trade-off between temporal and frequency resolution, making it less adaptive across modalities with varying signal characteristics. In contrast, CWT provides scale-adaptive time-frequency resolution, allowing it to preserve high temporal resolution for fast-changing components and high frequency resolution for slower dynamics. Although CWT introduces its own hyperparameters, we use the Mexican Hat wavelet, which has been shown to be effective in prior work on physiological signal analysis, as noted in Section 3.2.

While our original submission included the CLAP baseline, which uses STFT-based tokenization as part of its audio-focused design, we acknowledge that it differs from our core model in both architecture and pretraining assumptions. To address this concern more directly, we conducted an additional experiment using STFT-based tokenization within the NormWear architecture. This controlled comparison isolates the effect of the tokenization scheme. We present the results below and hope they provide further clarity on our design choice.

|Method|Activity Recognition|EEG Tasks|Risk Evaluation|Vital Signs|Micro Avg.|
|----------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| **NormWear - CWT** |**83.102**|**85.883**|**73.165**|**95.375**|**82.762**|
| NormWear - STFT 64 |76.555|79.565|64.153|94.425|76.403|
| NormWear - STFT 32 |74.656|78.706|64.934|94.910|76.141|
| NormWear - STFT 16 |74.494|76.459|63.694|94.701|74.917|

## 3) Though some parameters are shared across channels, forward pass still can be computationally costly under multi-channel scenarios.
Thank you for the observation. Our choice of a channel-independent design, where each channel is processed separately using a shared transformer backbone, follows insights from PatchTST [5]. This approach is well suited for self-supervised pretraining where input channel counts may vary between pretraining and fine-tuning. In contrast, channel-mixing designs depend on convolutional tokenizers with fixed kernel shapes, limiting flexibility in such settings.

Although channel-independent processing may seem more costly, it is parallelizable across compute resources, making it practical for deployment. We agree that optimizing efficiency is important, though it is beyond the scope of this work.

## 4) Unclear how text augmentation resolves nested relationships, improves representation quality, or justifies added training complexity in addition to direct categorical label supervision.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting these thoughtful concerns and provide the following clarifications.

First, our use of additional text modality is not aimed at directly resolving nested label structures. Rather, we incorporate rich textual prompts to mimic the semantic grounding observed in CLIP-style models, allowing the model to align physiological signals with semantic concepts for zero-shot inference. The nested label issue is addressed separately via a refinement module (Section 3.5, Appendix B.5), which uses Manhattan and cosine objectives to reduce confusion from overlapping class hierarchies.

Second, signal-text alignment is not intended to improve representation quality in the supervised setting. Its primary purpose is to enable semantic alignment for zero-shot use cases, which we believe is a valuable capability in wearable health applications (see our response to Reviewer qdb8).

Third, we provide traditional supervised evaluations using simpler categorical supervision via linear probing. As shown in Table 2 and Figure 5, NormWear consistently performs well under both supervised and zero-shot regimes.

Finally, the template-based text generation and LLM augmentation are performed once offline, so they introduce no additional computational overhead during deployment. Importantly, our inference-time complexity remains comparable to standard contrastive learning models in literature. We argue this added training complexity is warranted by the novelty and difficulty of enabling zero-shot inference on noisy physiological signals. 

## 5) Standard deviation across experiments and statistical analysis.
Regarding the standard deviation of the performance across experiments, we did report 5 fold cross validation performance with standard deviation in Table 13 in appendix on those downstream dataset with subject ID available. In addition, while conducting linear probing evaluation, classification tasks are solved by Newton's method with conjugate gradient, and regression tasks are solved by Cholesky's method, which could provide approximately closed-form solution, hence, yields highly stable results across repetitive evaluation runs.

The rank-based Critical Difference test we used (Appendix D) is a standard method that has been adopted in prior work [6]. Although it may be tempting to apply this test to individual datasets or tasks, it is not statistically valid when the number of evaluation points is small. We hope this clarification addresses the concern.

# Final comment
We thank the reviewer again for the constructive feedback. We also recognize the need for clearer presentation to avoid potential confusion around specific components such as the use of CWT or the perceived complexity. While these are important details, we hope they can be considered within the broader context of our contributions. These include, which are also gratefully acknowledged by all the reviewers, (i) the novel modeling strategy accommodating flexible numbers and types of sensor channels, (ii) the robust performance achieved across diverse health applications, and (iii) the fact that our entire work is open-sourced for the community. We hope this provides a more comprehensive view of our contributions and addresses the concerns raised. If there are aspects you feel could strengthen the contribution and support a more favorable assessment, we would appreciate any further guidance you may be willing to provide. 

# Reference
[1] Davide Anguita, Alessandro Ghio, Luca Oneto, Xavier Parra, and Jorge L. Reyes-Ortiz. A Public Domain Dataset for Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones.

[2] Zhang, X., Zhao, Z., Tsiligkaridis, T., & Zitnik, M. (2022). *Self‑Supervised Contrastive Pre‑Training For Time Series via Time‑Frequency Consistency*. In *Proceedings of NeurIPS 2022*.

[3] Mahardika T, Nurul Qashri, Yunendah Nur Fuadah, Da Un Jeong, and Ki Moo Lim. "PPG signals-based blood-pressure estimation using grid search in hyperparameter optimization of CNN–LSTM." Diagnostics 13, no. 15 (2023): 2566.

[4] Qin, Caijie, Yong Li, Chibiao Liu, and Xibo Ma. "Cuff-less blood pressure prediction based on photoplethysmography and modified ResNet." Bioengineering 10, no. 4 (2023): 400.

[5] Nie, Y., Nguyen, N. H., Sinthong, P., & Kalagnanam, J. (2023). *A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers*. arXiv preprint arXiv:2211.14730 (ICLR 2023).

[6] Pillai, Arvind, Dimitris Spathis, Fahim Kawsar, and Mohammad Malekzadeh. "Papagei: Open foundation models for optical physiological signals." arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.20542 (ICLR 2025).

# Response to Questions
## 1) Importance of zero-shot inference
We appreciate the reviewer’s interest in our zero‑shot evaluation. Evaluating models in a zero‑shot setting is both challenging and informative, as it tests whether pretrained models generalize beyond their training distribution. This is particularly relevant in clinical scenarios, where new diagnostic categories may arise. Unlike traditional supervised models that are limited to a predefined label set, our framework leverages the open-ended nature of text descriptions. This allows the model to produce predictions for novel categories by interpreting natural language labels, without needing to retrain on those new classes. Specifically, our approach aligns signal embeddings with text embeddings that capture semantic meaning, allowing the model to interpret input signals in terms of descriptive text rather than fixed class labels. This alignment enables zero-shot predictions by comparing signal representations with text descriptions of unseen categories. In turn, this supports flexible and scalable deployment in clinical contexts where label sets may evolve over time.

While zero-shot inference holds significant potential for real-world applications, it remains an under-explored research direction. We acknowledge the methodological and engineering challenges involved, but our goal is to take a first step toward this vision and offer a concrete direction and practical insight for future progress. In this study, we primarily use zero-shot inference as an evaluation strategy and encourage future work to also adopt this challenging setting to assess representation quality.

## 2) Importance of text augmentation
Thank you for this great question, text augmentation really is the linchpin of robust zero‑shot performance in our setting due to the nature of the available data. Most sensor datasets do not come with paired natural language descriptions, but instead contain only categorical labels (for example, "healthy" or "non-healthy") associated with signal segments. If using a fixed prompt such as "This subject is {healthy}" when training Normwear-Zeroshot, the model tends to overfit to the prompt structure rather than learning the semantics of the label, leading to AUC around 50–52 percent. By contrast, augmenting our text prompts teaches the model to disregard superficial wording and truly capture the meaning of each label, making it invariant to prompt phrasing and boosting zero‑shot accuracy.

On the other hand, CLAP was pretrained on 128,000 audio-text pairs that already cover a wide range of natural language expressions. From this perspective, CLAP has already seen the kind of linguistic variability that our text augmentation aims to simulate. Furthermore, during evaluation (inference), we used the same prompt for both CLAP and Normwear to ensure a fair comparison. We will revise our manuscript to further clarify this motivation.

# Response to Weakness
## 1) Result presentation of modality-specific baselines
We thank the reviewer for bringing this issue up. We have updated the table so that each entry in the `Modality-specific' column now indicates its corresponding model. In addition, we'd like to clarify that our goal for such comparison with modality-specific baselines is to position NormWear within the family of physiological foundation models, not to claim outright superiority over those modality-specific approaches. We show that a unified, multimodal model can achieve competitive results, outperforming specialist models on some tasks and trailing slightly on others, thereby validating the viability of a cross-modal framework. Detailed discussion tradeoffs between leveraging modality specific or generalist modeling approaches can be found under Result section 4.3, and our response to reviewer lush under section "Discussion of tradeoffs between modality-specific vs generalist approaches."

## 2) Clearer description of the novelty is needed
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out, and we agree that a clearer description of our novel contributions is needed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that demonstrates the feasibility of a single foundation model for multimodal wearable sensing physiological signals. Specifically, channel-aware attention with CLS token for modality agnostic multimodal physiological signals is one of the core innovations. It is designed to tackling the issue of taking varied number of sensing channels while still be able to extract cross-channel relationship during the encoding process; The choice of using CWT as initial signal embedding is another important contribution that is particularly well-suited for capturing sudden and time-varying changes in physiology (and superior to short term fourier transformation). Finally, our exploration on zero-shot capability is also considered a significant contribution in terms of proposing a desired evaluation scheme to test the quality of learned representation. 

# Final comment
We sincerely thank the reviewer once again for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. If there are aspects where our work could be further improved to merit a higher score, we would greatly appreciate any additional suggestions you might have.

### Figure 2:
The main structure of the backbone of NormWear is presented on the left. The model is pretrained following the standard masked autoencoder approach. Incoming sensor signals are transformed via continuous wavelet transform (CWT) into the initial multi-scale embeddings. These embeddings are then fed through alternating intra‑channel and inter‑channel encoder blocks in the backbone to extract high‑level latent representations while exchanging information across channels.

### Figure 3:
This module aggregate the sequence of representations, after the signal data pass through the backbone encoders, into a single fixed length embedding, according to three metrics: (i) relevance, which is conditioned by the semantic embedding of the question associated with the task of interest, (ii) recency, which is determined from the timestamp of each embedding, and (iii) importance, which is controlled by a gating function. The module is pretrained with contrastive learning to map the signal embedding, modulated by the prompted question, to the sentence of ground truth answer.

## 2) Question on variational-inspired approach
Thank you for the question, and we are sorry for the confusion on the notation we use. In our case, “variational-inspired” refers solely to our use of the reparameterization trick: after fusion we map the latent embedding to μ and σ via two linear layers, then sample $z = μ + σ \times ε (ε∼𝒩(0,I))$ for downstream alignment training. We do not perform full variational inference (e.g. no KL regularizer), so this is a stochastic sampling layer inspired by VAE rather than a true variational optimization over function spaces. 

## 3) Modality specific comment
Thank you for the question. Our goal is to position NormWear within the family of physiological foundation models, not to claim outright superiority over modality-specific approaches like PaPaGei (ICLR 2025). We show that a unified, multimodal model can achieve competitive results, outperforming specialist models on some tasks and trailing slightly on others, thereby validating the viability of a cross-modal framework. Detailed discussion tradeoffs between leveraging modality specific or generalist modeling approaches can be found under Result section 4.3, and our response to reviewer lush under section "Discussion of tradeoffs between modality-specific vs generalist approaches."

# Response to Weakness
## 1) Detailed formula of operations in cross-channel fusion
We agree with the reviewer that more equations would greatly help with the presentation of the proposed cross-channel fusion module. We added the following details in appendix ``G. Channel Fusion Complexity analysis":

### Operation of CLS fusion attention
We denote the input signals as $x$, where $x_i$ represents the $i$th channel. We denote the process of achieving initial embedding, including applying CWT operation, patching, and the first convolution layer, as $F_{init}$, then we have

$$F_{init}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times L \times E},  \text{s.t.  } F_{init}(x_i) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times E}$$

Where $N$ is the number of input sensing channels, $L$ is the patch size, and $E$ is the embedding size. We then denote the shared special token as $z=[CLS] \in \mathbb{R}^E$, and $z_i \in \mathbb{R}^E$ as the deep-copied version of special token being prepended at input channel $i$. After concatenation with the initial embeddings and pass through the first shared intra-channel encoder (self-attention layer), we will get the channel specific special token representation

$$z_i = softmax(\frac{Q(z) \cdot K(F_{init}(x_i))^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}) \cdot V(z),    \text{s.t.  }z_i \in \mathbb{R}^E$$

where $d_k$ is the dimensionality of the key vectors, and $Q, K, V$ are the linear mapping function of query, key, and value that is consistent with self-attention layer \citep{attn-all-you-need}. Then these channel specific special token representations will be further modulated through the inter-channel encoder

$$z_{all} = [z_1, z_2, ...] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times E}$$

$$z_{modulate} = softmax(\frac{Q(z_{all}) \cdot K(z_{all})^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}) \cdot V(z_{all}),    \text{s.t.  }z_{modulate} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times E}$$

where each channel specific special token representation in $z_{modulate}$ will be copied back to each channel and prepend to each of their corresponding $F_{init}(x_i)$, and the result embeddings will be then send to the shared intra-channel encoder in the second encoding block.

## 2) Detailed formula of operations in MSiTF
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion to describe the operations of our proposed module with more details. Regarding the operations of MSiTF, we added the following details in appendix ``B.4 MSiTF":

### B.4 MSiTF
Regarding the detailed forward operation, we aggregate the signal embeddings using a weighted average operation with weights determined from 3 aspects: relevance, recency, and importance, as specified in the following.

Relevance. With the semantic embedding of query sentence $q$ and backbone output $H \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times E}$, we have relevance being calculated as

$$W_{rel}(t) = cossim(q, k(H)) \in \mathbb{R}^L$$

where $k(\cdot) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times E}$ are the key linear mapping functions. 'cossim' is the function to compute cosine similarity between the query vector and each key vector which will result in a vector of length $L$ containing indicating relevance scores.

Recency. We also introduce recency score which is designed based on the assumption that the more recent the information, the more focus should be allocated. We define the recency score $W_{rec}$ of vector at each timestamp $t$ as an exponential decay function:

$$W_{rec}(t) = p^{T-t}, t \in (0, T), p <= 1$$

where $T$ is the total sequence length and $p$ is the decay factor. When $p=1$, the result score is equivalent to not considering the recency factor.

Importance. Finally, we consider the importance score in this case to be whether to keep the representation at each time step or not. The detail was presented in ``section 3.5 Sensor-Semantic Representation Alignment".

Integrated Score. The integrated weight $W$ is finally defined as:

$$W(t) = \frac{W_{rec}(t) + W_{rel}(t) + W_{imp}(t)}{\sum_{i=1}^T W_{rec}(i) + W_{rel}(i) + W_{imp}(t)}$$

which will result in the final output $\hat{Y} = \sum_{t=1}^T H_t \cdot W(t)$.

# Final comment
We thank the reviewer again for the thoughtful feedback. If there are any aspects where our work could be further improved to support a stronger evaluation, we would be grateful for any additional comments you might be willing to share.

Analogously, in NormWear, each modality-specific [CLS] token summarizes the latent context of its channel. This mechanism allows for a coordinated fusion of high-level representations, effectively aligning and regulating the downstream processing across modalities—mirroring the role of regulatory DNA sequences as integrative control units. Detailed operation of the [CLS]-token fusion is updated in response to reviewer CapQ under ``Operation of CLS fusion attention”. 
We recognize that a full theoretical motivation (e.g. formally proving its optimality or alignment properties) is beyond the scope of this work, and we view this as an important direction for future exploration.

We thank the reviewer for this constructive question. We agree that by visualizing the zero-shot prediction, we could better understand the behavior of the model while doing inference, hence, provide more insights on the potential interpretability. In Appendix I.5., we provide qualitative examples where the model responds to various task-specific textual queries in a zero-shot setting (e.g., detect seizure or detect eye closure, etc.). For each query, we visualize both the semantic relevance scores and the gating importance scores across time, demonstrating how the model adaptively attends to different parts of the input signal based on the nature of the task. This offers an interpretable perspective on the model’s preliminary ability to relate signal patterns to textual semantics in a zero-shot setting.

## 3) Discussion of tradeoffs between modality-specific vs generalist approaches.
We agree with the reviewer that a more holistic discussion on the trade-offs between modality-specific and generalist modeling approaches is needed. In the current manuscript, our discussion primarily focuses on downstream performance, while overlooking important aspects related to data preparation, pretraining, and deployment. We have therefore expanded our discussion on these limitations, as summarized below:

``While NormWear aims to generalize across diverse sensor modalities, this introduces several design and deployment trade-offs compared to modality-specific models. During training, generalist models require careful balance across modalities to prevent overfitting to dominant signal types, whereas modality-specific models can focus more narrowly on a single data distribution. This balancing process, however, exposes the model to richer and more varied signal patterns, potentially enabling broader generalization. In deployment, modality-specific models may be easier to fine-tune when the target modality remains fixed, but become cumbersome when extending to new sensor types. In contrast, NormWear’s generalist design supports more scalable deployment across heterogeneous signals without needing a separate model per modality, though fine-tuning still demands attention to cross-modal data balance. These trade-offs reflect a broader tension between specialization and adaptability in foundation model design for wearables. Future work could further explore modular or adaptive architectures to mitigate this tension and support both modality-specific refinement and cross-modal generalization."

# Response to Weakness
## 1) Use of Gumbel-trick Softmax
We thank the reviewer for bringing this issue up, we present our motivation here. We adopt the Gumbel-Softmax estimator to implement our gating mechanism as a discrete binary sampling process. By injecting Gumbel noise and annealing a temperature parameter, it yields near one-hot decisions while remaining fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end optimization of our gate parameters [1-2]. Although a standard softmax with a low temperature can similarly sharpen the output, it lacks the formal grounding in discrete sampling that the Gumbel-Softmax provides, and thus we favor its well-established theoretical and empirical validation [1-4].

## 2) Use of ClinicalTinyLlama
We chose ClinicalTinyLlama for its lightweight architecture, which underscores our framework's flexibility: practitioners can select a text encoder that matches their computational constraints and upgrade to more advanced models as they emerge (i.e. GPT-4). Moreover, ClinicalTinyLlama's pretraining on extensive clinical records makes it particularly attuned to health-specific terminology. We appreciate the reviewer's question about alternative encoders. Indeed, any high-quality model that clusters semantically similar sentences while separating dissimilar ones would perform well. In future work, we plan to explore unified embedding spaces (e.g., ImageBind) to further enhance the generalizability of our aligned representations.

We thank the reviewer again for the constructive feedback. If you feel there are areas where our work can be further improved, we would greatly value your additional feedback.

summary.value:
The authors present NORMWEAR, a foundation model tailored for multivariate, multi-modal physiological signals captured via wearable sensors. NORMWEAR addresses two main challenges:
1. Heterogeneous sensor configurations (varying modality, frequency, and number of channels),
2. Generalization across diverse health tasks (zero-, partial-, and full-shot).
The model includes:
* CWT-based tokenization for modality-agnostic preprocessing,
* Shared-weight intra-channel encoders and a novel channel-aware [CLS] token-based fusion for inter-sensor relationships,
* A memory stream inspired temporal fusion (MSiTF) module for semantic alignment with textual descriptions, enabling zero-shot inference.
NORMWEAR is pretrained on 2.5 million sensor segments and evaluated on 18 tasks across 11 public datasets. It demonstrates state-of-the-art results over baselines in zero-, partial-, and full-shot settings.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
1. The work is first of its kind to introduce a foundation model across heterogeneous wearable physiological modalities (ECG, EEG, IMU, etc.). The channel-aware [CLS]-token-based attention fusion and memory-inspired semantic alignment (MSiTF) are both well-motivated and technically novel.
2. The design includes clear architectural innovations: Tokenization via CWT+derivatives, Independent per-channel encoding to address sensor variability, Attention-based fusion across signal modalities, Relevance/recency/importance scoring in the MSiTF module.
3. Ablation studies and model variants (e.g., removing importance score, masking types, etc.) are thoroughly investigated.
4. Evaluations cover a wide range of tasks, modalities, and settings. Both macro and micro metrics are reported across 18 tasks, showing consistent improvement. Comparison against state-of-the-art domain-specific (e.g., PaPaGei, CBraMod) and general models (Chronos, TF-C, CLAP) is extensive.
5. The model supports arbitrary sensor setups without needing retraining. Zero-shot capability (via sensor-text alignment) is especially promising for real-world deployments where labeled data is sparse.

Weaknesses
1. While the architecture is sophisticated, there is little theoretical analysis of why the proposed fusion mechanisms work better. For instance, why [CLS]-based attention fusion outperforms mean-pooling is not analytically justified beyond empirical trends.
2. Some sections (e.g., MSiTF scoring mechanisms, derivation of gating weights) are dense and not clearly explained. Equation (1) uses Gumbel-softmax without adequately discussing why this is necessary over standard soft attention.
3. The use of a frozen TinyLlama clinical encoder is interesting, but not justified—would other encoders perform differently?

summary.value: In this paper, they propose a multimodal foundation model for sensor data. Unlike prior multimodal foundation models for sensor data, this does information sharing both between and within signals. Their approach has several steps: they curated a pre-training dataset from several sources, they develop a tokenization technique based on classical and recent approaches, they propose several approaches for sharing information within and between modalities and incorporate an alignment objective  to encourage alignment between sensor data embeddings and text descriptions. They show results, including zero-shot results on various downstream tasks with strong improvements over baseline.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strengths:
- This is actually a pretty comprehensive pipeline that seems relatively well thought out.
- There is very much a need for more foundation model techniques for wearables/mHealth.
- The combination of this pipeline and your application seem to be novel.
- The figures are not bad and are helpful.
- The results seem strong.

# Weaknesses:
- It would really help to have more equations, at least in the appendix. For instance, in 3.4 you mentioned several different fusion techniques. It would be much easier to understand them and what their stated limitations or benefits are if you gave some equations. You have a few e.g. equation 1 but far too few.
- Many of the citations are not the standard ones e.g. the original transformer and VAE papers. You should find their actual conference publications.
- You claim the first multi-modal and ubiquitous foundation model designed to extract generalized and informative representations from wearable sensing data. This is true if you only claim multimodal I believe, but you still need to cite [1].


Minor point: line 159 has afer, should be after

- The figures could really use captions. There is a lot going on in them and some hand-holding would be helpful. I get that there is a space limit, but in particular I look at the figures and if I want to skim them to get an idea of the paper, I don’t know what the most important things.
- “Once the signal embeddings are aggregated, we adopt a variational-inspired approach” what does this mean exactly? Variational refers to optimization over function spaces, and VAE is doing that for approximate posterior inference for latent variables. I don’t see how optimization over function spaces inspires your approach. Am I missing something??
- If I understand correctly, given your modality specific comment, are you beating e.g. PaPaGei (ICLR 2025)?

summary.value: The authors propose the NormWear foundation model for data collected from wearable sensors, such as smart watches. The model is pretrained on large datasets comprising multiple modalities of data, including PPG, EEG, and accelerometer data. They consider zero-shot, partial-shot, and full-shot evaluation on downstream evaluation data (unseen during pretraining) comprising many different tasks ranging from health-related tasks such as prediction of disease to human activity recognition. They demonstrate impressive performance in all three evaluation settings against multiple types of baselines, including models trained on handcrafted features, deep time series models, and foundation models for specific sensing modalities, such as PPG.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strengths
- Very thorough evaluation and comparison across many different datasets, prediction settings, and baselines. It meets the evaluation standard that I would expect for a paper focused on foundation models.
- Highly novel problem setting, as I am not aware of previous work on foundation models for multi-modal wearables data. I agree with the authors' argument on why this type of data is different from the type of data considered by deep time series models, as well as the need for modeling multiple modalities rather than having a foundation model for just a single modality.
- The proposed zero-shot evaluation seems to be a new and challenging evaluation setting for wearables data.

## Weaknesses
- Accuracy in full-shot evaluation compared to single modality foundation models is mixed. The results only partially support the claimed benefit of having a foundation model that incorporates multiple modalities.
- Novelty in the different components of the NormWear architecture is unclear. In the introduction, the novelty claim seems to suggest that the continuous wavelet transform-based transform, channel-aware attention, and human sensing adapted fusion mechanism are all new.
- Checklist is not completed properly. All justifications are listed as [NA]. The checklist is especially important for a paper like this that involves many existing datasets for pretraining and creating new assets. For example, item 12 on licenses for existing assets is not satisfied.
- Paper needs a thorough proofread for spelling and grammatical issues. The presentation is also unclear to me in many different areas.

Minor issues:
- Figure 5(b): Structued masking -> Structured masking
- Line 801: signal-sext alignment -> signal-text alignment

questions.value:
1. I have not seen zero-shot evaluation used on wearables data before and only have passing knowledge on its usage in other settings. What is an example of an application setting where zero-shot evaluation would be useful with wearables data?
2. Why is the text augmentation so crucial for the performance of zero-shot evaluation? Without it, the AUC for NormWear is only 50-52%, which is in the same range as CLAP and is essentially a random guess. Could adding such a text augmentation into CLAP lead to similar results as NormWear for zero-shot evaluation?

limitations.value: Limitations are discussed in the conclusion. The discussion seems to be adequate.

final_justification.value: After reading the other reviews and author rebuttals, I have increased my score from 3 to 4. Of the main weaknesses I identified in my review, one relates to the clarity, which the author rebuttals have helped with. I hope the authors will incorporate some of the discussions into the camera-ready paper, if accepted.

summary.value: The paper introduces normwear which is a multi-modal foundation model built to handle different wearable data, such as PPG, ECG, EEG, GSR, and IMU signals. It uses a channel-aware attention mechanism with a shared token to capture across-sensor patterns. The authors pretrained the model on a wide range of public datasets, and demonstrate generalization across 18 health-related tasks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
* The tokenization combines continuous wavelet transform (CWT) with signal differentiation, significantly increasing the dimensionality. It is unclear why the model needs explicit differentiation, as foundational models can learn such operations internally. This raises concerns about training and inference efficiency at scale.

* The authors use CWT instead of windowing, arguing it avoids fixed window functions, but CWT introduces its own hyperparameters (e.g., mother wavelet, scaling). Given the distinct frequency profiles of signals like ECG and PPG, it is unclear why a uniform scaling is applied or why this choice is better than using STFT.

* Despite time-series data’s similarity to audio, the authors do not benchmark STFT-based tokenization.

* Although all channels share the same transformer backbone, the forward pass runs separately per channel, which can be computationally costly, especially for multi-channel signals.

* Section 3.5 highlights challenges with nested relationships (e.g., stress vs. depression, running vs. cycling) in contrastive learning, but the paper does not clarify how the proposed approach (additional text modality without labels) solves this well-known problem. While CLIP-style alignment works well for visual-text pairs where the image-text correspondence is often rich and intuitive, it’s less clear why aligning time-series signals (like EEG, ECG, IMU) to natural language labels should yield better representations. Signals are often low-level, noisy, and not easily or inherently describable in human language, so this alignment may introduce unnecessary abstraction or noise. This setup also adds multiple layers, i.e., sentence template generation, large language model augmentation, and text embedding matching, which significantly increases complexity. The paper doesn’t clearly explain whether simpler label supervision (e.g., direct categorical labels) performs worse or why the extra linguistic layer is essential.

* Standard deviation or variability across experiments is not reported, even though some baselines yield close performance, making it hard to assess statistical significance in specific datasets. While the authors provided statistical significance on the model comparison in Appendix D, it is not detailed for each application.

Overall, the paper employs several techniques without fully explaining the motivations or providing ablation studies, adding to the method's complexity without clear justification.

questions.value:
1) Line 801, B.6 Sentence template example for signal-sext alignment. Typo?

2) PPG-DaLiA dataset: The original manuscript reports ~36 hours of data, but Table 5 lists 71 hours for pretraining. Could the authors explain this discrepancy?

3) Appendix Fig. 15, Q4: The question asks, “Is this an area with tumor?” — is this meant to refer to a specific EEG channel or the full multi-channel EEG signal? Why do the authors assume a specific patch can reveal tumor-related features rather than considering the full temporal context?

4) Sampling rate mismatch: Since the signals have different sampling rates and the tokenization does not standardize them, does the model learn features specific to each sampling rate?

final_justification.value:
My key concerns remain unresolved.

1. **CWT with Derivatives**: The use of first- and second-order derivatives alongside CWT adds considerable computational and dimensional overhead. The justification is weak, cited works are application-specific and do not support this design for a general-purpose foundational model. This choice appears ad hoc rather than principled.

2. **Sampling Rate**: Resampling all signals to 65 Hz is questionable for modalities like ECG and EEG, which contain important information above this range. This decision risks discarding signal content critical for downstream performance.

3. **Channel Adaptivity**: The “channel-adaptive” design is simply channel-independent processing with a shared backbone, a straightforward implementation, not a meaningful architectural contribution.

4. **Manuscript Quality**: Numerous typos remain, indicating a lack of careful proofreading.

Given the limited novelty, unresolved technical concerns, and presentation issues, I believe the manuscript requires substantial revision and do not recommend acceptance.

title.value: Toward Foundation Model for Multivariate Wearable Sensing of Physiological Signals

TLDR.value: NormWear: A Normative Foundation Model that Learns Representations of Multimodal Wearable Sensing Signals for Diverse Digital Healthcare Applications

abstract.value: Time-series foundation models excel at tasks like forecasting across diverse data types by leveraging informative waveform representations. Wearable sensing data, however, pose unique challenges due to their variability in patterns and frequency bands, especially for healthcare-related outcomes. The main obstacle lies in crafting generalizable representations that adapt efficiently across heterogeneous sensing configurations and applications. To address this, we propose NormWear, the first multi-modal and ubiquitous foundation model designed to extract generalized and informative representations from wearable sensing data. Specifically, we design a channel-aware attention mechanism with a shared special liaison [CLS] token to detect signal patterns in both intra-sensor and inter-sensors. This helps the model to extract more meaningful information considering both time series themselves and the relationships between input sensors. This helps the model to be widely compatible with various sensors settings. NormWear is pretrained on a diverse set of physiological signals, including PPG, ECG, EEG, GSR, and IMU, from various public datasets. Our model shows exceptional generalizability across 11 public wearable sensing datasets, spanning 18 applications in mental health, body state inference, vital sign estimation, and disease risk evaluation. It consistently outperforms competitive baselines under zero-shot, partial-shot, and full-shot settings, indicating broad applicability in real-world health applications.

See https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and ensure all material is anonymized. The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22)

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.

Responses are confidential and will not be shared with reviewers, area chairs, or senior chairs. The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
